# About these notes {#sec-about .unnumbered .web-only}

Lecture notes for *Near-term Quantum Computing* (UvA, 2026-2027), one chapter per
lecture. Chapters are added as the course goes on.

## How to use these notes {.unnumbered}

- **Chapters.** Each chapter follows one lecture and goes into more detail than the
  lecture can. [On the website, the exercises of all chapters are also collected on the
  [Exercises](exercises.qmd) page, with links back to the chapters.]{.content-visible when-format="html"}
- **Glossary.** Underlined terms are explained in the [Glossary](glossary.qmd). On the
  website, hover over a term (or tap it on a phone) to see its definition, and click it
  to open the glossary.
- **Search.** The search box at the top of the sidebar searches all chapters; on a
  computer, the shortcut is `/`.
- **PDF.** The download icon next to the title gives all published chapters as one
  PDF, with the same numbering, for printing or reading offline. Glossary terms are in
  italics there, and the glossary is an appendix.

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

The notes assume basic quantum mechanics and the circuit model: Dirac notation, Pauli
matrices, density matrices, expectation values and their statistical error.

The tutorials are Jupyter notebooks in Python, which run in Google Colab. They assume
basic Python (variables, functions, loops, lists and dictionaries) and a little
familiarity with Jupyter notebooks, NumPy arrays and Matplotlib plots. If any of these
is new to you, these short introductions cover what we need:

- Python: the official [Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/),
  sections 3 to 5;
- Jupyter notebooks in Colab: [Overview of Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/basic_features_overview.ipynb);
- NumPy: [NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html);
- Matplotlib: [Quick start guide](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/quick_start.html).

## Tutorials {.unnumbered}

Each notebook opens in Google Colab. To keep your work, use **File → Save a copy in
Drive** before you start. If you prefer to work in your own environment, download the
notebook instead. New notebooks and solutions appear in this table as they are
released.
